name: Comites Taifali (palatina)

abilities.name: Rapid Advance
abilities.text: Improved unit movement speed over an extended period.

abilities.name: Flying Wedge
abilities.text: The unit moves into a flying wedge-shaped attack formation.

abilities.name: Trample
abilities.text: Charges are more effective for an extended time.

attributes.name: Disciplined
attributes.text: This unit does not suffer a morale penalty when the general dies. It can also rally after routing more often.

attributes.name: Scare (everyone)
attributes.text: This unit frightens all enemy units.

attributes.name: Immune to Fear
attributes.text: This unit is immune to the fear effects of scary units.

short: The Taifali, a tribe most likely belonging to the Ostrogothic group or to the Sarmatians, were famous for their excellent cavalry. The Taifali are first mentioned in the 3rd century AD; it is believed that they lived in the lower Danube, on its northern bank, next to the Victohali tribe. This was an area of interaction between the Germanic peoples and the Sarmatians, and the timing of the settlement of the Taifals fits perfectly into the phase of tribal integration and mixing in the northern Balkans. They accompanied the Gothic king Сniva in his campaigns against Moesia and Dacia in the 3rd century A.D. The Taiphali participated in many conflicts of the 4th century, both on the side of the Empire and against Rome. After Emperor Constantine defeated the Goths, the Taifals continued to attack the Romans until they were pacified in 336. The Taifals received the status of Roman foederati and were allowed to occupy Oltenia (western Wallachia), but not all of them became part of the Empire: some of the tribe refused to resettle on Roman lands. Perhaps the Romans allowed this because they did not want to mess with the harsh mountainous region or needed a buffer to cover their borders from nomadic attacks. In addition to the various detachments bearing the name of Taifali listed in the Notitia Dignitatum, there is also the praefectus Sarmatarum et Taifalorum gentilium Pictavis in Galia – «the prefect in charge of the Sarmatian and Taifalian settlers in Gaul».
history: One of the simplest forms of one-armed catapult, the onager relied on twisted skeins of animal sinew which provided the power to hurl either rocks or shot. Inaccurate but powerful, it was an effective siege machine against buildings and fortifications, but was of far less use on the battlefield unless firing into massed infantry ranks. First mentioned by Philon of Byzantium in his treatise on ‘Mechanics’, the onager made use of a sling-like cradle attached to a firing arm. This arm was inserted, twisted, and propelled rocks or shot through torsion. As the firing arm was released, the sling-like cradle would unhook, firing the projectile. A padded beam was incorporated into the housing frame to restrain the arm. Larger machines could require as many as eight or ten crewmen, and the incredible recoil meant that they could not be easily or safely mounted on walls or towers. Quickly constructed wherever wood was readily available, onagers soon became a staple of ancient siege warfare.
strengths: Very low damage and armour penetration
